lesson.intro.title: What is Hangul?
lesson.intro.0: Hangul (한글) is the Korean alphabet, created in 1443 by King Sejong so that anyone could learn to read. It has 24 basic letters: 14 consonants (자음) and 10 vowels (모음).
lesson.intro.1: Letters are not written in a line like English. They stack into square syllable blocks — one block = one syllable. Read each block left → right, top → bottom.
lesson.intro.3: Every block has at least one consonant and one vowel. When a syllable starts with a vowel sound, the silent ㅇ fills the consonant spot: 아 = a, 이 = i.
lesson.intro.4: In the next lessons you will meet every vowel and consonant, build blocks yourself, then learn the few rules that change how words sound. Tap any letter to hear it.
lesson.vowels.title: Basic vowels
lesson.vowels.0: Vowels are built from three strokes: a dot for the sky (ㆍ), a flat line for the earth (ㅡ) and a standing line for a person (ㅣ). Today the dot is written as a short stroke.
lesson.vowels.1: Add a second short stroke and you add a "y" sound: ㅏ a → ㅑ ya, ㅓ eo → ㅕ yeo, ㅗ o → ㅛ yo, ㅜ u → ㅠ yu.
lesson.vowels.3: Tall vowels (ㅏ ㅑ ㅓ ㅕ ㅣ) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant: 가. Flat vowels (ㅗ ㅛ ㅜ ㅠ ㅡ) sit BELOW it: 고.
lesson.consonants.title: Basic consonants
lesson.consonants.0: The five core consonants are pictures of how your mouth makes the sound: ㄱ the tongue root blocking the throat, ㄴ the tongue tip on the gum ridge, ㅁ the closed mouth, ㅅ a tooth, ㅇ the open throat.
lesson.consonants.2: An extra stroke means a stronger sound. Learn the 5 base shapes and the other 9 follow.
lesson.tense.title: Plain, aspirated, tense
lesson.tense.0: Korean has three versions of several consonants. Plain sounds are soft, aspirated ones release a puff of air, and tense ones (the doubled letters) are tight with no air.
lesson.tense.2: Tissue test: hold a tissue in front of your mouth. Aspirated sounds make it move; tense sounds keep it still.
lesson.tense.4.title: Hear the difference
lesson.compound.title: Compound vowels
lesson.compound.0: The remaining 11 vowels are combinations of the basic ones — read the parts and glide them together.
lesson.compound.2: Shortcuts: ㅐ and ㅔ sound the same for most speakers today, and ㅙ ㅚ ㅞ all sound like "we".
lesson.build.title: Build a syllable
lesson.build.0: Where each letter goes depends on the vowel: tall vowels go right of the consonant, flat vowels go below, and combined vowels wrap around. A final consonant (받침) always goes at the bottom.
lesson.batchim.title: Final consonants
lesson.batchim.summary: Only 7 sounds at the end of a block
lesson.batchim.0: A consonant at the bottom of a block is a 받침 (batchim). Many letters can sit there, but at the end of a syllable they collapse into just 7 sounds.
lesson.batchim.2: Double finals (ㄳ ㄵ ㄶ ㄺ ㄻ ㄼ ㄽ ㄾ ㄿ ㅀ ㅄ) are usually read as just one of the two: 값 → [갑] gap, 닭 → [닥] dak, 앉다 → [안따] anta.
lesson.rules.title: Reading rules
lesson.rules.summary: Why words sound different from spelling
lesson.rules.0: Korean is spelled by meaning, so a few sound changes happen when blocks meet. [Brackets] show how a word is actually said.
lesson.rules.1.title: Linking (연음): a final slides into a following ㅇ
lesson.rules.2.title: Nasalization (비음화): k/t/p before ㄴ ㅁ → ng/n/m
lesson.rules.3.title: ㅎ + plain → aspirated (격음화)
lesson.rules.4.title: Silent ㅎ between vowel sounds
lesson.rules.5.title: ㄴ next to ㄹ → ㄹㄹ (유음화)
lesson.rules.6.title: Tensing (경음화): after k/t/p, the next consonant tightens
lesson.rules.7: That is all of Hangul. You can now sound out any Korean word — go practice it in the stages!
tip.v_eu: eu — say "oo" with lips spread flat
tip.v_ae: ae — "e" as in "bed" (mouth a little wider)
tip.v_e: e as in "bed" (same as ㅐ for most speakers)
tip.c_giyeok: g at the start, k at the end — softer than English k
tip.c_digeut: d at the start, t at the end
tip.c_rieul: a light tap between r and l; l at the end
tip.c_bieup: b at the start, p at the end
tip.c_siot: s as in "sun" (sh before ㅣ: 시 = shi)
tip.c_ieung: silent at the start, ng at the end
tip.c_chieut: ch with a strong puff of air
tip.c_kieuk: k with a strong puff of air
tip.c_tieut: t with a strong puff of air
tip.c_pieup: p with a strong puff of air
tip.c_ssanggiyeok: kk — tight throat, no air: like "k" in "sky"
tip.c_ssangdigeut: tt — tight, no air: like "t" in "stop"
tip.c_ssangbieup: pp — tight, no air: like "p" in "spy"
tip.c_ssangjieut: jj — tight, no air: like "ts" in "cats"
app.0.useFor: Walking, subway and bus directions, opening hours and reviews.
app.0.tip: Google Maps cannot give full walking or driving directions in Korea — locals use Naver Map. Switch the app language to English in settings.
app.1.useFor: A second map app with great real-time bus arrival info.
app.1.tip: Handy for checking when your bus arrives at a stop.
app.2.useFor: Subway route planner for Seoul, Busan, Daegu, Gwangju and Daejeon.
app.2.tip: It tells you which train car to board for the fastest transfer or exit. On Android, search "KakaoMetro" in Google Play.
app.3.useFor: Calling taxis — the way most people get a cab in Korea.
app.3.tip: Set your destination in the app so you do not need to explain it to the driver.
app.4.useFor: Korean ↔ English translation, including camera mode for menus and signs.
app.4.tip: Point the camera at a menu to translate it instantly.
app.5.useFor: Booking high-speed KTX trains between cities.
app.5.tip: Seoul → Busan takes about 2.5 hours by KTX. Book ahead on weekends and holidays.
app.6.useFor: Official tourism guide: events, attractions and travel info.
app.6.tip: Call 1330 any time for free tourist help with interpreters.
hist.0.story: The first Korean kingdom. Its founding by Dangun is celebrated every 3 October as National Foundation Day (개천절).
hist.1.story: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest and Silla in the southeast competed for the peninsula, and Buddhism spread widely.
hist.2.story: Silla unified most of the peninsula. Its capital Gyeongju left treasures like Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto.
hist.3.story: The name "Korea" comes from Goryeo. Famous for celadon pottery and some of the world's earliest metal movable type.
hist.4.story: A Confucian dynasty ruled from Seoul. King Sejong created Hangul in 1443 and announced it in 1446 — celebrated on Hangul Day, 9 October.
hist.5.story: Joseon became an empire and tried to modernise under growing foreign pressure.
hist.6.story: Korea was annexed by Japan. The 1 March 1919 independence movement (삼일절) is remembered as a national holiday.
hist.7.story: Liberated in 1945 (광복절, 15 August), the peninsula was divided. The Korean War (1950–1953) ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty.
hist.8.story: Industrialisation turned South Korea from one of the poorest countries into a major economy — the "Miracle on the Han River".
hist.9.story: Mass protests won democratic elections in 1987, and Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics.
hist.10.story: Korean dramas, music, films, food and beauty spread worldwide — which may be why you are learning Hangul right now!
food.0.why: Grilled at your table, wrapped in lettuce with garlic and sauce.
food.0.where: Barbecue alleys everywhere — Mapo in Seoul is famous.
food.1.why: Thin slices of beef marinated in sweet soy sauce, then grilled.
food.1.where: Everywhere — Eonyang (Ulsan) and Gwangyang have famous local styles.
food.2.why: Sweet soy-marinated pork ribs grilled at your table.
food.2.where: A classic at neighbourhood barbecue restaurants nationwide.
food.3.why: Korea's prized native beef, richly marbled — grilled simply with salt.
food.3.where: Hoengseong in Gangwon is famous for its hanwoo.
food.4.why: Chewy, savoury and crispy — a late-night favourite with soju.
food.4.where: Wangsimni's gopchang alley in Seoul; Daegu's Anjirang alley for the pork version.
food.5.why: Rice topped with vegetables, egg and chili paste — mix it all.
food.5.where: Jeonju is the bibimbap capital of Korea.
food.6.why: Crispy fried pancakes, best with makgeolli rice wine.
food.6.where: Gwangjang Market in Seoul, also known for mini gimbap.
food.7.why: Chewy rice cakes in sweet-spicy sauce — the classic street snack.
food.7.where: Sindang-dong in Seoul has a whole tteokbokki street.
food.8.why: Chicken, cabbage and rice cakes stir-fried in a big pan.
food.9.why: Hearty pork broth over rice — a local favourite.
food.9.where: Busan is the home of dwaeji gukbap.
food.10.why: A whole young chicken stuffed with rice and ginseng.
food.10.where: Koreans eat it on the hottest summer days for energy.
food.11.why: A whole chicken simmered with garlic into a mild, healing broth — finished with rice porridge.
food.11.where: Restaurants by mountain streams, a summer outing classic.
food.12.why: Double-fried for extra crunch, plain or glazed — with beer it is 치맥 (chimaek).
food.12.where: Chicken shops on every street, and delivery until late.
food.13.why: Crispy chicken pieces tossed in a sticky sweet-spicy glaze — great cold too.
food.13.where: Traditional markets — Sokcho's Jungang Market is famous for it.
food.14.why: Sausage filled with glass noodles and blood — the street-food partner of tteokbokki.
food.14.where: Sillim-dong's Sundae Town in Seoul (stir-fried) and Byeongcheon near Cheonan.
food.15.why: Chewy noodles in icy broth — refreshing in summer.
food.15.where: Found at naengmyeon specialists and BBQ restaurants.
food.16.why: A famous local breed, grilled like Korean BBQ.
saju.0.title: Korean Saju reading
saju.0.desc: Your Four Pillars of Destiny read from your birth date and time — personality, strengths and the year ahead.
saju.1.title: Saju couple compatibility
saju.1.desc: How your two birth charts match — love, communication and harmony through Korean saju (궁합).
conv.greetings.title: Hello & introductions
conv.greetings.situation: Meeting someone for the first time.
conv.greetings.tip: A small bow with your greeting is polite. Koreans often ask your age early on — not to be nosy, but to know which level of politeness to use.
conv.greetings.l3: I'm Emma. I'm from the US.
conv.greetings.k2: I'm from Canada (swap in your country)
conv.cafe.title: Ordering at a café
conv.cafe.situation: Ordering a drink at the counter.
conv.cafe.tip: Koreans love iced americano so much it has a nickname: 아아 (a-a). Many people drink it iced even in the middle of winter.
conv.cafe.l5: To go. Can I pay by card?
conv.restaurant.title: At a restaurant
conv.restaurant.situation: Getting a table, ordering and paying.
conv.restaurant.tip: There is no tipping in Korea. Side dishes (반찬) and water are free and refillable, many tables have a call button, and you usually pay at the counter on your way out.
conv.restaurant.l2: Excuse me! Could we have a menu?
conv.restaurant.l6: That was delicious! The bill, please.
conv.shopping.title: Shopping & prices
conv.shopping.situation: Buying clothes at a market stall.
conv.shopping.tip: Friendly bargaining is fine at traditional markets, but not in department stores or chain shops. Prices use Sino-Korean numbers: 만 = 10,000, 천 = 1,000.
conv.shopping.l2: Could you give me a discount?
conv.shopping.l3: Then I'll give it to you for 13,000 won.
conv.shopping.l5: Yes, we have black and white.
conv.directions.title: Asking for directions
conv.directions.tip: Subway exits are numbered — locals give directions like "exit 3". Korean map apps are far more accurate here than international ones.
conv.directions.l0: Excuse me. Where is the subway station?
conv.transport.title: Taxi & subway
conv.transport.situation: Taking a taxi, then the subway.
conv.transport.tip: One rechargeable transit card works on buses and subways, and transfers within about 30 minutes are discounted. Keep seats marked for elderly or pregnant passengers free.
conv.transport.l5: Does this train go to City Hall station?
conv.convenience.title: Convenience store
conv.convenience.situation: Paying for snacks and a lunch box.
conv.convenience.tip: Korean convenience stores are a food destination: look for 1+1 and 2+1 deals, triangle gimbap and instant noodles you can cook at the hot-water station inside.
conv.convenience.l4: Do you have a points card?
conv.politeness.title: Polite vs casual speech
conv.politeness.situation: Saying the same thing to different people.
conv.politeness.tip: Ending sentences with 요 is your safe default. Switch to casual 반말 only when the other person invites you to — using it uninvited with someone older can come across as rude.
conv.politeness.l3: Have you eaten? (casual — also a greeting)
conv.politeness.k2: You can speak casually with me
conv.friends.title: Making friends
conv.friends.situation: Getting to know someone your age.
conv.friends.tip: Age decides what you call each other: women say 언니 / 오빠 to older women / men, men say 누나 / 형. Since 2023 Korea officially uses international age, though many people still mention the old counting.
conv.friends.l2: You're older than me — my unnie!
conv.friends.l4: Sure! Can you give me your number?
conv.friends.l5: Sure, let's hang out next time!
conv.fans.title: Concerts & fan events
conv.fans.situation: At a concert and a fan signing event.
conv.fans.tip: 화이팅 ("fighting") means "you can do it!". At concerts fans shout organised fan chants and sing along together (떼창) — learning the chant is part of the fun.
conv.drama.title: Words from K-dramas
conv.drama.situation: Casual reactions you hear in every drama.
conv.drama.tip: These are casual (반말) — great with friends, but too blunt for strangers, teachers or anyone older.
conv.drama.k0: What do I do?! / Oh no!
conv.pharmacy.title: Pharmacy & hospital
conv.pharmacy.tip: Pharmacies are everywhere — look for the big 약 sign. For an ambulance call 119, and 1330 is a free tourist helpline with interpreters.
conv.pharmacy.l2: Since yesterday. I have a fever too.
conv.pharmacy.l3: Take this medicine three times a day.
conv.pharmacy.l4: Do I take it after meals?
conv.hotel.title: Hotel check-in
conv.hotel.tip: In traditional guesthouses (한옥 stays) you take your shoes off inside and may sleep on floor mattresses heated from below (온돌).
conv.hotel.l0: I'd like to check in. I have a reservation.
conv.emergency.title: Emergencies & help
conv.emergency.situation: Asking for help when something goes wrong.
conv.emergency.tip: Police: 112. Fire & ambulance: 119. Both can connect an interpreter. Lost items are often handed in — ask at the station or a police box (파출소).
conv.emergency.l4: Is there anyone who speaks English?
conv.emergency.k2: I need to go to a hospital
conv.dining.title: Eating & drinking etiquette
conv.dining.situation: Dinner and drinks with Korean friends.
conv.dining.tip: Wait for the eldest to start eating. Pour drinks for others (never yourself) holding the bottle with two hands, and turn your head slightly away from elders when you drink.
conv.dining.l0: Thank you for the meal! (before eating)
